intro.title: It’s OK to ask
paragraphs: You’re moving things on Saturday and don’t have enough hands. Asking feels awkward: it seems like being a burden.
You try to ask in a way that makes it easy for the person both to agree and to say no.
Choose what to say. If an answer doesn’t work, you stay where you are, see the reaction and understand why.
intro.note: The other person’s styles are patterns of behaviour, not types of people: the same person acts differently on different days. Real people react differently, so this is practice with wording, not a prediction.
intro.disclaimer: A learning simulation. The material draws on well-known communication methods (sources are given at each step), but it has not yet been reviewed by a psychologist.

variants.name: Busy and brief
variants.desc: Speaks briefly, is in a hurry, values specifics.

variants.name: Kind but unsure
variants.desc: Wants to help but is afraid of not managing.

nodes.narr: You’re moving on Saturday and don’t have enough hands. You need to ask someone you know for help, and you’ve met for coffee to ask.
nodes.ask: How do you start the request?

options.text: I need help on Saturday: I’m moving and need a hand for 2–3 hours from 11 a.m. Can you?
options.why: A clear request says what, when and how much. It’s easier to answer “yes” or “no” when the scope is clear.

direct.say: Saturday, 11 a.m.… Let’s see.

evasive.say: Oh, a move! So what exactly needs doing?

options.text: Sorry to bother you again, you probably have a lot on, but maybe it’ll work…
options.why: Apologising in advance and offering a way out yourself sounds like “asking is awkward”. The request loses weight, and “no” is practically suggested.

direct.say: If you think so, maybe better not.

evasive.say: Well, if it’s inconvenient, let’s not.

options.text: Please help, I really need it.
options.why: A vague request makes the other person guess how long it will take. An unknown scope often brings a cautious “no”.

direct.say: Need what? Say it properly.

evasive.say: Help with what? I didn’t get it.

options.text: Nobody will help me, but fine, I’ll at least ask you.
options.why: This makes the other person your “last chance” and puts them in a guilty position. It’s pressure, not a request.

direct.say: Great, now you’re holding a grudge too.

evasive.say: Oh, that sounds like a reproach.

tech.name: A clear request
tech.text: A request is clear when it names the specific action, time and scope, without hints or apologies.

nodes.hint: What does the person need to know to answer honestly: what, when, how much?

direct.say: I’m listening. I have about fifteen minutes.

evasive.say: Hi! Did something happen? You look worried. I’m swamped today, though.

nodes.narr: The other person hesitates and delays answering.

options.text: If it doesn’t work out, that’s fine. I want your honest answer.
options.why: Saying out loud that they can refuse increases the chance of agreement and the honesty of the answer: the person doesn’t feel cornered.

direct.say: Then honestly: I can help a bit, let’s see.

evasive.say: Thanks for saying that. Let’s think about what I can definitely help with.

options.text: Oh please, what’s it to you!
options.why: Pressure turns the talk into persuasion. Agreement under pressure usually leaves the person with a bad aftertaste and you with a feeling of debt.

direct.say: It’s exactly this kind of pressure that makes me not want to.

evasive.say: Please don’t push, I already feel awkward.

options.text: We’ve always helped each other, so you’ll help me too.
options.why: Reminding someone of debts turns help into a calculation. A request stays a request as long as the answer can be “no”.

direct.say: Was that a reproach just now?

evasive.say: You think I owe you?

options.text: Fine, forget it. I’ll manage somehow.
options.why: Leaving in a huff closes the topic and damages the relationship. You never learn what the person could have offered.

direct.say: Fine. Whatever you want.

evasive.say: Oh, don’t be upset…

tech.name: The right to say no
tech.src: Carpenter, Social Influence, 2013 («But you are free»)
tech.text: A phrase that gives the person back their freedom of choice has been shown in studies to increase agreement without harming the relationship.

nodes.hint: How to give the person freedom to say “no” without weakening the request?

direct.say: Saturday is packed. I don’t know.

evasive.say: Oh, I’d like to, but I’m afraid I’ll just get in the way…

nodes.narr: The other person is ready to help, but not fully.
nodes.ask: How do you respond to a partial “yes”?

options.text: An hour will help a lot too. Let’s do this: at 11 we carry out the heavy furniture together.
options.why: A partial yes is worth accepting and putting straight into the plan. A specific task for that hour makes the help useful.

direct.say: Good, I’ll take the heavy stuff at 11.

evasive.say: The heavy stuff, right? I can do that. Agreed, 11.

options.text: An hour? Then maybe it’s not worth it.
options.why: By rejecting part of it, you lose everything. A little help is often more important than it seems.

direct.say: As you say. So, no.

evasive.say: Then sorry I even agreed.

options.text: An hour is nothing, make it at least two.
options.why: Bargaining right after agreement devalues it. The person has already named their limit.

direct.say: I said an hour. I didn’t choose two.

evasive.say: But I said: only for an hour.

options.text: Thanks, an hour works.
options.why: Accepting the offer is already good. Stronger: add what exactly you’ll use that hour for — that seals the agreement.

direct.say: OK. Then at 11.

evasive.say: Fine, at 11.

tech.name: Accept a partial “yes”
tech.text: A realistic agreement is better than a perfect answer: take what the person is ready to give and define the task.

nodes.hint: What to do when they agreed to only part of it?

direct.say: I can only do an hour. No more.

evasive.say: I can do an hour, no more… Will that even help?

nodes.narr: The other person offers an exchange.

options.text: I’d be glad to help you in return. Tell me when it suits you.
options.why: Being ready to reciprocate makes the help equal. Relationships rest on exchange, not debt.

direct.say: Deal. I’ll let you know.

evasive.say: Good. That makes me feel easier.

options.text: You don’t need to return anything, it’s nothing.
options.why: Refusing reciprocity can devalue your exchange and leave the person with a sense of debt they can’t settle.

direct.say: Well, if it’s nothing, then fine.

evasive.say: Oh, it’s still awkward.

options.text: No, no, there’s no need, I’ll manage somehow.
options.why: You just asked for help, and now you’re refusing an exchange. This confuses the other person.

direct.say: Make up your mind.

evasive.say: Wait, aren’t you the one asking for help?

options.text: Help isn’t a free service — expect to return the favour.
options.why: A cold phrase makes the relationship look like a deal. Reciprocity is better expressed with warmth.

direct.say: Sounds like a condition.

evasive.say: Oh, that’s harsh.

tech.name: Reciprocity
tech.text: The norm of reciprocity: people like knowing help can be returned. It strengthens the bond.

nodes.hint: How to show help is mutual without turning it into a deal?

direct.say: OK. And later maybe you’ll help me with something.

evasive.say: Well… if anything, you’ll help me sometime too, right?

nodes.narr: The conversation is coming to an end. All that’s left is to say thank you.

options.text: Thank you, your willingness really helps. I’ll text you on Friday to confirm the time.
options.why: Specific thanks names what exactly mattered and seals the agreement with a next step.

direct.say: Great. I’ll wait for your message.

evasive.say: Deal. Text me on Friday.

options.text: Finally we agreed.
options.why: These words sound like a reproach for the long bargaining. Thanks should be about the person, not the conversation.

direct.say: What do you mean, “finally”?

evasive.say: That sounded like a reproach to me.

options.text: I could have managed without you too.
options.why: This phrase takes value away from someone’s help and spoils the impression.

direct.say: Then why ask?

evasive.say: I see. Then maybe it’s not needed?

options.text: OK, bye.
options.why: Leaving without thanks and without a specific step leaves the agreement vague.

direct.say: Bye.

evasive.say: Well, talk later.

tech.name: Specific thanks
tech.text: Name what exactly helped and why it matters: that way thanks strengthens the relationship instead of staying a formality.

nodes.hint: What to say so the person feels their help matters?

direct.say: OK. Anything else?

evasive.say: Fine. Do you need anything else?

direct.say: Deal. See you on Saturday.

evasive.say: OK, I’ll come. Text me on Friday.

finale.title: It’s OK to ask
finale.lead: The request was clear and free, and it ended with a specific agreement. Here’s what it relied on:
carry: Asking specifically: what, when, how much.
Leaving the person the right to say no.
Accepting a partial “yes” and anchoring it with a task.
finale.prompt: What request are you putting off? Write it down as one specific sentence.
